los.text: Recognise the bones that comprise the orbit
los.html:
WallBonesClinical
RoofFrontal (orbital plate), lesser wing of sphenoidAnterior cranial fossa above
FloorMaxilla, zygoma, palatineBlowout fracture (thinnest with the medial wall): infraorbital nerve numbness, trapped inferior rectus
Medial wallEthmoid (lamina papyracea, paper-thin), lacrimal, maxilla (frontal process), sphenoidOrbital cellulitis spreads from ethmoid sinusitis
Lateral wallZygoma, greater wing of sphenoidStrongest
Seven bonesFrontal, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal, maxilla, zygomatic, palatine.
OpeningsOptic canal (apex), superior and inferior orbital fissures, nasolacrimal canal.

los.text: Locate the superior orbital fissure and name the structures that pass through it
los.html:
• Superior orbital fissure: gap between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid.
Passes throughAbove the common tendinous ringThrough the ring
NervesLacrimal, frontal (V1), trochlear (IV)Oculomotor (III) (superior and inferior divisions), nasociliary (V1), abducens (VI)
VeinsSuperior ophthalmic vein (to the cavernous sinus)
Mnemonic("Lazy French Tarts Lie Naked In Anticipation")Lacrimal, Frontal, Trochlear, (Lateral → Superior division III), Nasociliary, Inferior division III, Abducens.
Superior orbital fissure syndromeIII, IV, V1, VI lesions together → ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, numb forehead.

los.text: Name the muscles of the orbit, their actions and innervations
los.html:
MusclePrimary actionNerve
Superior rectusElevation (also adduction, intorsion)III
Inferior rectusDepression (also adduction, extorsion)III
Medial rectusAdductionIII
Lateral rectusAbductionVI
Superior obliqueDepression in adduction (and intorsion, abduction)IV
Inferior obliqueElevation in adduction (and extorsion, abduction)III
Levator palpebrae superiorisRaises upper eyelidIII (+ sympathetic: superior tarsal muscle)
LR6 SO4, rest 3.
Clinical testing (H pattern)
  • in abduction, superior and inferior recti act as pure elevator/depressor
  • in adduction, the obliques do (superior oblique looks down and in).
Origins
  • Four recti from the common tendinous ring around the optic canal
  • Superior oblique from the sphenoid body, passes through the trochlea
  • Inferior oblique from the orbital floor (only one not from the apex).

los.text: Identify the branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve and recognise their functions
los.html:
Branch of V1Supplies
Frontal → supraorbital, supratrochlearForehead, scalp to the vertex, upper eyelid, frontal sinus
LacrimalLacrimal gland area, lateral upper eyelid (carries parasympathetic fibres from VII to the lacrimal gland)
Nasociliary → long ciliary, anterior and posterior ethmoidal, infratrochlear, external nasalCornea (long ciliary: afferent limb of the corneal reflex), ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses, side and tip of the nose
Hutchinson's signShingles vesicles on the tip of the nose (nasociliary) predict eye involvement.
Corneal reflexAfferent V1 (nasociliary), efferent VII (orbicularis oculi).

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the optic nerve and chiasm
los.html:
Optic nerveAxons of retinal ganglion cells; actually a CNS tract (oligodendrocytes, wrapped in meninges with CSF around it).
Course
  • From the back of the eyeball
  • → through the orbit within the cone of muscles
  • → optic canal (with the ophthalmic artery)
  • → middle cranial fossa
  • → optic chiasm above the pituitary.
ChiasmNasal fibres cross (they see the temporal fields); temporal fibres stay on the same side → optic tracts.
ClinicalPapilloedema (raised ICP transmitted along the nerve sheath), optic neuritis (MS), compression at the chiasm (pituitary tumour → bitemporal hemianopia).
Central retinal arteryBranch of the ophthalmic artery running in the nerve; an end artery (occlusion → sudden painless monocular blindness, cherry-red spot).

los.text: Describe the arterial supply and venous drainage of the orbit
los.html:
SupplyDetail
Arterial
  • Ophthalmic artery (first branch of the ICA) through the optic canal → central retinal artery, ciliary arteries, lacrimal, supraorbital, supratrochlear, ethmoidal arteries
  • Anastomoses with ECA branches on the face
VenousSuperior and inferior ophthalmic veins → cavernous sinus (also pterygoid plexus and facial vein); valveless
  • Clinical: infection on the face (the "danger triangle") can spread via valveless ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus → cavernous sinus thrombosis.

los.text: Describe the origins, courses and functions of the oculomotor, trochlear and abducent nerves and predict the consequences of injury to them
los.html:
NerveOriginCourseSuppliesLesion
Oculomotor (III)Midbrain (in front, between cerebral peduncles)
  • Between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
  • → past the PCom artery
  • → lateral wall of cavernous sinus
  • → SOF (in the ring)
SR, IR, MR, IO, LPS; parasympathetic to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle (ciliary ganglion)
  • Down and out, ptosis, dilated pupil (compressive lesions affect the outer pupillary fibres first: PCom aneurysm, uncal herniation)
  • Diabetes often spares the pupil
Trochlear (IV)Midbrain, back (only one), crossesLongest intracranial course → lateral wall of cavernous sinus → SOF (above the ring)Superior obliqueVertical diplopia, worse looking down and in (stairs, reading); head tilt away from the lesion
Abducens (VI)Pontomedullary junctionLong climb over the petrous apex → inside the cavernous sinus beside the ICA → SOF (in the ring)Lateral rectusCan't abduct, horizontal diplopia worse looking to that side; false localising sign of raised ICP

los.text: Describe the anatomical relations of the cavernous sinus and common pathologies relating (anatomically) to it
los.html:
• Cavernous sinus: venous sinus on each side of the sella turcica (pituitary) and body of the sphenoid, from the SOF to the petrous apex.
PositionStructures
Lateral wall (top → bottom)III, IV, V1, V2
Inside the sinusInternal carotid artery (with its sympathetic plexus), VI (beside the ICA)
MedialPituitary, sphenoid sinus
  • Drains: ophthalmic veins, sphenoparietal sinus → superior and inferior petrosal sinuses → IJV
    • links to the pterygoid plexus and facial veins (valveless).
PathologyFeatures
Cavernous sinus thrombosis (spread from facial or sinus infection)Proptosis, chemosis, painful ophthalmoplegia (VI first), numb forehead/cheek (V1, V2), fever; can spread to the other side
Carotid–cavernous fistula (trauma)Pulsatile proptosis, bruit, red eye
ICA aneurysm in the sinusVI palsy, then other nerves
Pituitary tumour growing sidewaysCranial nerve palsies

los.text: Identify the ciliary ganglion and its branches and recognise consequences of pathology to it and its branches
los.html:
• Ciliary ganglion: parasympathetic ganglion lateral to the optic nerve, near the orbital apex.
RootFibresEffect
Parasympathetic (from III, inferior division)Synapse here → short ciliary nervesSphincter pupillae (constriction) and ciliary muscle (accommodation)
Sympathetic (from the ICA plexus)Pass through without synapsingDilator pupillae (mostly via long ciliary nerves)
Sensory (from nasociliary)Pass throughCornea and eyeball
Adie's (tonic) pupilGanglion damage → large pupil reacting slowly to light, better to near.
Light reflex efferent runs through it: III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves.
Horner's(sympathetic loss)Ptosis (superior tarsal), miosis, anhidrosis; not a ciliary ganglion lesion.

los.text: Recall the route of the visual pathways from the eye to the occipital lobe and link to the functional consequences of damage at different points along that pathway
los.html:
1. RetinaNasal and temporal halves. Each half sees the opposite visual field.
2. Optic nerveOptic chiasm: nasal fibres cross.
3. Optic tractLateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus).
4. Optic radiationsMeyer's loop (lower fibres, upper field) through the temporal lobe; upper fibres (lower field) through the parietal lobe.
5Primary visual cortex (occipital lobe, calcarine sulcus).
Lesion siteField defect
Optic nerveMonocular blindness (same eye)
Optic chiasm (pituitary tumour)Bitemporal hemianopia
Optic tractContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Meyer's loop (temporal lobe)Contralateral upper quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky")
Parietal radiationsContralateral lower quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor")
Occipital cortex (PCA stroke)Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (dual MCA supply)

los.text: Identify the parts of the eye
los.html:
LayerPartsFunction
Fibrous (outer)Sclera (white, opaque), cornea (clear front, most refractive power)Protection, shape, focusing
Vascular (uvea)Choroid (behind), ciliary body (ciliary muscle: accommodation; ciliary processes: aqueous humour), iris (pupil size)Nourishes retina, focusing, light control
InnerRetina: photoreceptors (rods, cones), macula and fovea (sharpest vision, cones only), optic disc (blind spot)Detects light
ContentsLens (held by suspensory ligaments / zonules), aqueous humour (anterior and posterior chambers), vitreous body
Aqueous humour
  • Made by the ciliary body
  • → posterior chamber
  • → through the pupil
  • → anterior chamber
  • → drains at the iridocorneal angle (trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm).
  • Blocked → raised intraocular pressure (glaucoma).
AccommodationCiliary muscle contracts → zonules relax → lens rounds up for near vision.
